mad_001: You can recognise it by the buttressed trunk and feathery foliage of a Mexican wetland cypress, standing in formal Spanish planting. It stands in the Jardin del Parterre, and Madrid calls it El Abuelo, the grandfather.
mad_002: You can recognise it by the dark, tiered branches of a deodar cedar. It stands directly in front of the pond at the Palacio de Cristal, the glass and iron pavilion of 1887, and frames the usual postcard view of it.
mad_003: You can recognise it by the three separate trunks, 142, 120 and 140 centimetres round, fused into one crown 18 metres wide, and by the wooden fence around it. It stands against the eastern wall of the Palacio de Velazquez.
mad_004: You can recognise them by the trunks standing in the water itself, with the cypress knees breaking the surface around them. They grow calf deep in the pond in front of the Palacio de Cristal, not on the bank beside it.
mad_005: You can recognise it by its height, 32 metres and the tallest tree in the garden, on a trunk a metre and a half across. It stands on the Plano de la Flor terrace, and it is the Mediterranean cypress there.
mad_006: You can recognise it by its height, over 30 metres, and by what it is: a Caucasian zelkova, a relative of the elms without being one. It stands in the garden's north zone along the Paseo de Mutis, catalogued as singular tree 260.
mad_007: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.6 metres round, under a crown 18.5 metres across. It stands alone at the centre of the Glorieta del Trillo in Casa de Campo, where three roads meet and the roundabout is named after it.
mad_009: You can recognise it as the Atlas cedar that people here call El Abuelo, the grandfather. It stands beside the artificial stream in the northern part of Parque del Oeste, near the Fuente de la Salud.
mad_010: You can recognise it by where it grows, half hidden among shrubs rather than out in the open. It stands beside the Casa del Cura, the small hermitage in El Capricho, and it is the stone pine there.
mad_012: You can recognise it by the flat horizontal plates of branches and a crown 22 metres across on a tree 26 metres tall, so nearly as wide as it is high. It stands beside the Velazquez statue, by the Prado's busiest door.
mad_013: You can recognise it as the one broadleaf among the square's four catalogued conifers, 25 metres tall on a smooth grey trunk. It stands in the Plaza de Murillo, at the corner of the Museo del Prado.
mad_014: You can recognise it by the side branches hanging almost vertically, carrying the longest needles of any spruce, so the tree looks like it is melting. It stands in the Plaza de Murillo, between the Prado and the Botanic Garden.
mad_015: You can recognise it by the trunk splitting into four stems at about head height, and by the leaf undersides, pale silver white, so a breeze changes the colour of the whole crown. It stands in the Jardines de Cecilio Rodriguez.
mad_016: You can recognise it by its height, 33 metres, and a crown still conical at the top while it spreads below, where the Prado cedar is flat topped. It stands where the Avenida del Peru meets the Plaza de Guatemala.
mad_017: You can recognise it by the bark peeling away in long ribbons and by the initials carved into the trunk, which is too wide to get your arms halfway round. It stands north of the Estanque Grande, near the Paseo de Coches.
